Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants
M. A. Rigsby, L. J. Brogan, N. V. Doubina, Y. Liu, E. C. Opocensky, T. A. Spurlin, J.
Zhou, and J. D. Reid
Lam Research Corporation, 11155 SW Leveton Dr., Tualatin, Oregon 97062, USA
Conventional damascene electroplating utilizes a combination of
organic additives, namely, a suppressor, an accelerator, and a
leveler, to achieve superconformal fill of interconnects. An
alternative mechanism for superconformal cobalt fill is proposed
here. This mechanism, the Differential Current Efficiency Fill
(DCEF) mechanism, utilizes sacrificial oxidants to achieve void-
free superconformal fill. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of
a sacrificial oxidant, such as H<sup>+</sup>, O<sub>2</sub>, or an organic additive,
promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between the field
and the feature bottom. Addition of a single suppressor-type
additive assists in driving the plating rate differential. By
appropriately selecting the sacrificial oxidants, organic additives,
the waveform, and the mass transport conditions, void-free
superconformal cobalt fill can be achieved in a variety of features.
Introduction
As interconnect dimensions continue to decrease, the extendibility of conventional
copper damascene processing becomes increasingly problematic, in terms of yield and
reliability. Small feature openings require thin seed to avoid having them close before the
features can be filled (pinch-off) due to large overhang formation during seed deposition.

nucleation during the electrodeposition process. Reliability is also impacted by the
decreasing line dimensions (1-2). Due to the higher current density in smaller lines, void
formation occurs more readily, leading to decreasing electromigration lifetime as critical
dimensions scale down. A third issue with decreasing dimensions is increasing RC delay
and IR drop due to the exponential increase in resistivity with decreasing line cross-
section (1-2). As such, the space occupied by the barrier layer within the feature becomes
much more valuable.

Superconformal cobalt fill does not follow the conventional damascene process,
with suppressors, accelerators, and levelers. Rather, it can be achieved using a single
organic additive. Previous studies have investigated the effect of various additives on
cobalt fill in sub-micrometer trenches and through-silicon vias (4-6). Fill is typically
attributed to a potential-dependent suppression effect that results in an S-shaped negative
differential resistance. However, this mechanism may not hold for very small dimensions,
on the order of tens of nanometers, as the ability to bifurcate into active and passive
regimes is dependent on electrode dimensions (7-8).
New insights are presented for superconformal cobalt fill in nanometer-scale
features through a proposed mechanism that the authors have termed the Differential
Current Efficiency Fill (DCEF) mechanism. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of
one or more sacrificial oxidants promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between
the field and the feature bottom by directly altering the deposition rate through current
efficiency. Suppressor-type additives may promote the plating rate differential either by
altering the kinetics of deposition or by behaving as a sacrificial oxidant, or both. It will
be demonstrated that this strategy can be applied to achieve superconformal cobalt fill in
nanometer-scale features.

Results and Discussion
Figure 1 demonstrates void-free bottom-up fill of high-aspect-ratio features with cobalt.
Such superconformal fill has been achieved in a variety of feature dimensions. The
mechanism by which bottom-up fill proceeds is quite different from that of the
conventional copper damascene process. As such, the cobalt plating bath consists of only
one additive, a suppressor-type organic species.
Figure 1. Bottom-up progression of cobalt fill of cobalt-seeded structures. Bath
contained Suppressor A.
To explore the mechanism that leads to superconformal cobalt fill, a series of
electrochemical tests were done in combination with electrochemical quartz crystal
microbalance (EQCM) experiments. Figure 2 compares the electrochemical and
corresponding EQCM responses during a slow-sweep cyclic voltammogram at pH 2.5
and pH 4.0. The electrochemical data gives information about the suppression strength of
the additives, but is complicated by the competing hydrogen evolution reaction and
possible effects of pH on additive behavior, and so this type of data has only limited
value. Because the EQCM is sensitive to mass change during the electrochemical process,
it gives direct information on the amount of cobalt deposited under a given set of
conditions, which is crucial when the system has competing reactions. In comparing these
two plots, it is observed that the total current at a given potential is generally greater at
the lower pH, but the cobalt partial current is greater at the higher pH. It can be
concluded that hydrogen evolution is in strong competition with cobalt deposition and
that it is, therefore, consuming a significantly greater portion of the current at lower pH.

A - Echem pH Effect - Suppressor A
Figure 2. A) Electrochemical response during cyclic voltammogram in presence of
Suppressor A at pH 2.5 and pH 4.0. B) EQCM response during the cyclic voltammogram
shown in A. 10 mV/s, no stirring.
From the data in Figure 2, current efficiency is an important factor in
electrodeposition of cobalt. To further investigate this effect, EQCM experiments were
done over a range of pH and current density. In Figure 3, the current efficiency derived
from the EQCM has been plotted as a function of (A) the current density and (B) the
potential. From Figure 3A, the current efficiency decreases with decreasing current
density, and this effect is significantly enhanced by decreasing pH. Because both the
onset of hydrogen evolution occurs at lower overpotential than that of cobalt deposition
and the hydrogen evolution reaction kinetics are faster, current efficiency is low at the
lower current densities (9). At high current density, the cobalt reduction dominates and
the current efficiency is high.
From the plot of current efficiency as a function of the potential (Figure 3B), the
presence of a suppressor-type additive is shown to play an important role in increasing
the potential window over which hydrogen evolution occurs without significant cobalt
reduction. Thus, the current efficiency for cobalt deposition can be modulated by a
suppressing additive. From numerous fill tests on various structures, it is found that
bottom-up fill occurs under conditions that lead to lower current efficiency (i.e., lower
current and lower pH). The addition of a suppressing organic promotes this behavior.

Deposition rate is another factor that must be considered. Because this
information is not as obvious from the voltammetric plots of Figure 2, Tafel plots were
generated. Figure 4 presents Tafel plots based on the EQCM-derived cobalt partial
current density at pH 2.5 and pH 4.0, both with and without Suppressor A in solution.
The first feature that stands out is that the charge transfer coefficient is changed by the
presence of the additive. This is as expected, because a suppressor-type additive should
affect the reaction kinetics. This effect of the additive on the reaction kinetics is critical
because of its impact on current efficiency. On the other hand, the charge transfer
coefficient is not affected by changing pH. This means that the effect of pH on the cobalt
deposition rate is not kinetic, but it rather must be thermodynamic, which is not expected
for the direct deposition of a metal. However, the change in thermodynamics of
deposition is clearly demonstrated in the plots. The onset potential for cobalt reduction,
both with and without additive, shifts by ~-59 mV/pH, which is consistent with a reaction
mechanism where hydroxide is involved. Under these test conditions, the cobalt
deposition reaction must proceed as consecutive 1-electron transfer steps through a cobalt
hydroxide intermediate (10). Altering the pH then leads to modification of the deposition
rate due to the changing hydroxide ion concentration.
Figure 4. Tafel plots generated from EQCM data for cobalt deposition showing the effect
of pH and additive. 10 mV/s, no stirring.

From the data above, it is concluded that pH plays an important role in
determining not only the current efficiency for cobalt deposition, but also the
thermodynamics of the deposition process. However, this does not fully explain the
phenomenon of bottom-up fill in interconnects. To produce bottom-up fill, there must be
a significant differential in the deposition rate between the field and the feature bottom.
In Figure 5, Tafel plots are again presented, this time with varying potential scan
rate at two different pH. At slow scan rate and with no solution stirring during the
potentiodynamic deposition, the system approaches an approximate steady state, meaning
that the near-surface region is essentially at equilibrium. By increasing the scan rate, the
system can be pushed further away from the steady-state condition, and changes in
deposition rate may become observable through comparison of the potential shift
between the forward and reverse scans. At slow scan rate, pH 2.5 and pH 4.0 exhibit a
similar shift in potential that is due to the pH shift that comes from the mass-transport
limited depletion of
\mathrm { H } ^ { + }
near the electrode surface. Under the non-equilibrium conditions
of high scan rate, however, a significant increase in the potential shift is observed at low
pH, while the shift is unaffected at higher pH. Because the current efficiency is
significantly lower at the lower pH, the proton concentration change is larger and the
local pH shift during the potential scan is greater. By not allowing the system to reach
equilibrium during the scan, it becomes apparent that significant pH differences, and
therefore, deposition rate difference, may be possible within a single system.

, organic additive) quickly develop within the feature due to
the low current efficiency. The concentration gradients lead to a difference in current
efficiency, thermodynamic deposition rate, and deposition kinetics between the base of
the feature and the field. Bottom-up fill is then driven by the gradient-induced
differentials and proceeds up the feature until the transport-induced concentration
gradients are dissipated. At this point, fill shuts down, everything is equally suppressed,
and deposition continues slowly and conformally. Because of the critical reliance on
current efficiency to produce bottom-up fill, this mechanism has been termed the
Differential Current Efficiency Fill mechanism (DCEF).
Organic suppressor-type additives have been found to be crucial to achieving
efficient bottom-up fill through the DCEF mechanism. The additives can play multiple
roles in the fill process. By altering the kinetics of the deposition reaction, the additive
can significantly lower the current efficiency, which maintains a very slow deposition
rate on the field and assists in generating the pH gradient within the feature. Consumption
of the organic additive within the feature would also generate an additive concentration
gradient under the lower mass transport conditions, which decreases the overall
suppression within the feature relative to on the field. Finally, depending on the pK<sub>a</sub> of
the particular additive, its adsorption properties could be altered, further driving the
field/base deposition rate differential.

The reliance on current efficiency-induced pH and additive gradients leads to
some important implications for the DCEF mechanism. As an example, for high-aspect
ratio features, the evolution of fill will be dependent on the current density that is selected.
At very low current density, H<sup>+</sup> and additive will be depleted near the base of the feature
only. This will lead to bottom-up deposition, but the fill will shut down too deep within
the feature due to the depth of the H<sup>+</sup>/additive depletion zone. At higher current density,
the H<sup>+</sup>/additive depletion zone will be at a shallower location within the feature, which
could lead to undesirably fast deposition on the sidewalls and, therefore, pinch-off and
seam formation. If the current density is high enough, the current efficiency will be too
high to support formation of the appropriate concentration gradients, and deposition will
be conformal rather than bottom-up. Thus, for deep features, stepping the current up
during the fill process can assist in moving the depletion zone to more appropriate depths
so that bottom-up fill can continue to completion.
A similar effect would be expected when simultaneously filling features of
varying dimensions. For the feature for which the process conditions were optimized, fill
will be bottom-up and void-free. However, because the H<sup>+</sup>/additive depletion zone
depends strongly on the current, the rotation rate, and feature depth, different feature
dimensions will fill differently for the given process conditions. Significantly deeper
features will likely pinch off and form a seam because the depletion zone is too high in
the feature, while significantly shallower features may not fill at all because the depletion
zone is too deep. Careful selection of proper waveform, mass transport, and
concentrations is therefore critical to achieving superconformal growth across a die.
Conclusions
Superconformal cobalt fill is achieved in high-aspect ratio nanometer-scale features by
effective use of sacrificial oxidants through the DCEF mechanism. The sacrificial oxidant
may be, for example,
\mathrm { H } ^ { + } , \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,
, or an organic additive and functions to lower the cobalt
deposition current efficiency. By operating at low current efficiency, concentration
gradients for the active sacrificial species are developed within the feature. Here, the role
of
\mathrm { H } ^ { + }
as a sacrificial oxidant has been demonstrated. In addition to shifting the reaction at
the base of the feature toward cobalt deposition through higher relative current efficiency,
it has been shown that shifts to higher pH via
\mathrm { H } ^ { + }
consumption and lower mass transport
lead to faster cobalt deposition rates through the thermodynamics of a
\mathrm { C o O H } ^ { + }
reaction
intermediate. Relatively small pH shifts, which can be achieved through mass transport
effects, can lead to significant differences in deposition rates. Due to their impact on the
deposition kinetics, suppressor-type additives play an important role in lowering the
current efficiency at a given potential, driving the pH gradient formation and limiting
plating on the field. Additive gradients, either through concentration gradient formation
or through the effect of pH shifts on adsorption and suppression properties, can also
create a differential in kinetics within the feature. Bottom-up cobalt fill proceeds when
waveform, mass transport, and organic and inorganic solution constituent concentrations
synergistically create the appropriate deposition rate differential through the DCEF
mechanism. The DCEF mechanism and insights presented here may be applicable to
superconformal fill of other metals, as well.
